title: Linear Causal Representation Learning by Topological Ordering, Pruning, and Disentanglement
claim: The method iteratively peels off one latent variable at a time, estimating it and projecting out its effect, until all are recovered.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, legend bar on top, green arrows between stages
description: A wide figure with a legend bar across the top (causal edge, noise variable z, latent feature y, observation x). Below are three dashed rounded panels read left to right, one per iteration. Each panel has a small latent causal graph on top (y1, y2, y3) and below it a layered diagram: noise z to latent y (orange arrows), then blue arrows from y to observations x1–x4 inside a dashed box. Green arrows labeled 'Remove the causal effect of y1' and then 'y2' lead to the next panel. In later panels, nodes and edges become dashed circles as they are eliminated, and the remaining variables are projected (Π⊥ x). Under each panel, α-hat feeds into the estimates ỹ and ẑ, with the ẑ estimate looped back by a green arrow.
caption: An illustration of subroutine 1. Dashed nodes and edges are eliminated.
abstract: Causal representation learning (CRL) has garnered increasing interest from the causal inference and artificial intelligence communities due to its potential to disentangle complex data-generating mechanism into causally interpretable latent features by leveraging the heterogeneity of modern datasets. In this paper, we further contribute to the CRL literature, by focusing on the stylized linear structural causal model over latent features and assuming a linear mixing function that maps latent features to the observed data or measurements. Existing linear CRL methods often rely on stringent assumptions, such as access to single-node interventional data or restrictive distributional constraints on latent features and/or exogenous measurement noise. However, these prerequisites can be easy to violate in practice. In this work, we propose a novel linear CRL algorithm that, unlike existing methods, operates under weaker assumptions on environment heterogeneity and data-generating distributions while still recovering latent causal features up to an equivalence class. We further validate our new algorithm via synthetic experiments and an interpretability analysis of large language models, demonstrating both its superiority over competing methods in finite samples and its potential in integrating causality into understanding artificial intelligence. The source code is available at https://github.com/utulie/code_for_linear_crl_paper_creator.
